(TATYANA MAKEYEVA) Overnight strikes killed 12 people in Russia and Ukraine, authorities said Sunday, as waves of drones and missiles pummelled civilian infrastructure on both sides. With fighting at the front at a near standstill and talks frozen, the warring countries have significantly stepped up long-range attacks deep behind each other's lines, pushing the civilian death toll to its highest levels since the war's first months in 2022. In Russia, swarms of Ukrainian drones killed five people in a residential area of the southern Rostov region, regional governor Yuri Slusar said. Two more people were killed in the Belgorod and Moscow regions. Advertisement Advertisement Moscow regional governor Andrey Vorobyov described the assault as "one of the most massive drone attacks in recent memory". Russia's defence ministry said it had intercepted 822 drones across the country overnight. In Ukraine, a barrage of Russian drones and missiles killed two people and wounded 14 at ArcelorMittal's steel plant in Kryvyi Rih, President Volodymyr Zelensky's hometown. The plant, one of Ukraine's biggest steel producers, said it partially halted operations after the strike damaged its core production facilities. Strikes also hit other regions, killing two people in the southeastern Zaporizhzhia region and one in the border region of Sumy. In Kyiv, a popular outdoor book market at Pochaina, long the place to find rare and antiquarian volumes, was struck. Bookseller Dmytro Semenukha saw all four of his stalls burn to the ground. Advertisement Advertisement "There used to be a store. And books, and flags of all the countries, all the countries. Tons of everything. And that's it," the 45-year-old told AFP. In a social media post on the overnight raid, Zelensky said "wherever the Russians can reach with their ballistic missiles, they strike civilian infrastructure." Over the past week, he said, Ukrainian cities had been pummelled by "more than 1,550 attack drones, nearly 1,560 guided aerial bombs, and 62 missiles", as he renewed his appeal to allies for more air defence. - Spillover to Europe - Russia has carried out near-daily missile and drone strikes across Ukraine since launching its full-scale invasion in early 2022. It has recently intensified attacks using hard-to-intercept ballistic missiles, exploiting Ukraine's air-defence shortages after the US-Israeli war against Iran diverted supplies. Advertisement Advertisement "When North Korean ballistic missiles destroy infrastructure and claim lives here in Europe, European interceptors cannot simply be allowed to sit in storage," Zelensky said. Kyiv has recently renewed claims that Moscow is receiving more missiles and troops from its ally North Korea. Countries bordering the conflict have meanwhile faced increasing spillover from the drone war. After the overnight raid, Romania's defence ministry said a Spanish F-18 fighter jet shot down a drone that breached its airspace near the borders with Ukraine and Moldova. NATO said Friday its fighter jets shot down a drone that entered Latvian airspace -- the second such incident there in a week, according to Latvia's defence ministry. For its part, Ukraine has increasingly targeted warehouses belonging to Russia's biggest online retailer Wildberries, saying the company supplies components for Russian drones. Advertisement Advertisement Near Moscow, another Wildberries warehouse was set ablaze by Ukrainian drones overnight. Since mid-July, Ukraine has struck around 20 warehouses and buildings linked to the company. Zelensky says those strikes, along with attacks on oil refineries, are aimed at undermining Russia's war economy. In July alone, 437 civilians were killed in Ukraine, the highest monthly toll since May 2022, according to a United Nations tally. Photograph: Ronaldo Bolanos/Los Angeles Times/Getty Images Los Angeles LA woman charged with murder over bus crash that preceded deadly helicopter plunge Bailee Lynn Rios, 36, accused of driving on wrong side of road to cause fatal crash NBC news helicopter was covering Uwa Ede-Osifo Thu 17 Sep 2026 20.34 EDT Last modified on Thu 17 Sep 2026 20.35 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A California woman was allegedly driving under the influence when she sped down the wrong side of the road, ran a red light and plowed her SUV into a Los Angeles metro bus on Tuesday, killing two passengers, prosecutors say, in a tragedy compounded when a news helicopter covering the crash plummeted from the sky, killing three. Bailee Lynn Rios, 36, has been charged with two counts of murder over the deaths of the two people on the bus, identified as Daniel Castillo, 46, and Gage Weida, 31. Rios was being held on $4.1m bail and is set to be arraigned on 18 September. Online court records did not list a lawyer who might speak on her behalf, and the public defender’s office did not immediately return a message about whether it was representing her. The wake of Tuesday’s deadly bus crash took a turn for the worse in the hours after, when a local news helicopter responding to the scene crashed to the ground in a fiery ball, killing two individuals onboard: pilot George Marciniw and reporter Eliana Moreno. A pedestrian on the ground, 29-year-old Edy Gutierrez Mejia, also died in the crash. Reached Wednesday, Rios’s mother, Cindy, said she was shocked and saddened by the string of events. She said she had not spoken to her daughter since her arrest and had not been contacted by law enforcement. She could not immediately be reached on Thursday for additional comment. Castillo left behind four children. “We are still trying to process the unimaginable reality that he is no longer with us,” his youngest daughter, Johaunna, wrote on a fundraising page for funeral expenses. Weida’s family planned to visit him for his 32nd birthday, his father told CBS LA. “Unfortunately, we’re still heading out there, but for all the wrong reasons,” said Jeffrey Weida. “The deadly and destructive consequences of her actions will be felt for years to come,” Los Angeles county district attorney Nathan Hochman said in a statement. Stephanie Wiggins, chief executive of the Los Angeles metro, extended her sympathies to the bus crash’s victims and their families. “We are grateful to the first responders who rushed to the scene and to the law enforcement investigators and prosecutors working to establish the facts and pursue justice,” she said in a statement. View image in fullscreen The aftermath of the helicopter crash in Chatsworth, Los Angeles on Tuesday night. Photograph: Kayla Bartkowski/Los Angeles Times/Getty Images A vigil was planned Thursday evening to honor the victims of both crashes. There were no immediate details on what caused the helicopter to go down, but investigators said significant clues could come from the last seconds of video the crew broadcast. In it, an alarm could be heard inside the helicopter’s cockpit as it lost altitude. National Transportation Safety Board investigator Fabian Salazar said on Wednesday the video was “probably the most important evidence that we have discovered so far”. In the video, after the beeping starts, a woman’s voice says: “Uh oh.” The helicopter moves quickly away from the bus crash site and starts losing altitude. The woman says, “You can’t pull up?” before the video stops as the chopper nears the ground. Aviation safety expert Jeff Guzzetti said the alarm suggested a potential loss of engine power and a dangerous decrease in the main rotor speed. He said the pilot appeared to be trying to perform an emergency maneuver to use the wind to force the rotor to spin again. The NTSB is also investigating the bus collision. Moreno and Marciniw worked for Angel City Air, a helicopter contractor, and provided aerial coverage for NBC4 and Telemundo 52. Moreno, born in Orange county, joined Angel City Air in 2010, the same year she earned a broadcast journalism and political science degree from Chapman University. She reported for several news outlets and began flying with Marciniw in 2023, NBC4 said. Marciniw grew up in southern California and graduated from Burbank high school in 1974. There have been at least eight fatal crashes involving news helicopters in the US since 2000, killing 16 people, according to a review of federal accident records and news accounts. https://www.euronews.com/2026/10/01/us-d.text: Tennessee death row inmate Christa Pike was taken to hospital on Thursday after authorities "failed" to carry out her execution, her lawyers said, with witnesses reporting the convicted murderer was breathing despite two injections intended to kill her.Just hours earlier the US Supreme Court cleared the way for Pike to be the first woman to die by lethal injection in the southern US state of Tennessee in 200 years.Tennessee corrections officials did not publicly confirm the outcome of the execution, which included two injections of pentobarbital."Tonight the State of Tennessee once again failed to carry out a lawful execution," Pike's attorneys said in a statement."Christa is being treated at a nearby hospital. We have not been informed as to her condition."Pike was scheduled for execution at 10:00 am (1700 CET) at the Riverbend Maximum Security Institution, where witnesses including journalists were present for the administration of the injections."It appears this did not go how this was supposed to go," said investigative journalist John North of WBIR who was a witness at the execution site, adding "when we left the building, so far as we knew, she was probably still alive."During the livestream, an ambulance with its lights flashing could be seen leaving the site of the execution, it's unclear if it was transporting Pike.The execution procedure went ahead hours after the US Supreme Court ruled that it could proceed, with liberal justices Sonia Sotomayor, Elena Kagan and Ketanji Brown Jackson all dissenting."The Court's decision...unnecessarily prevents that [lower] court from giving due consideration to Pike's claim," the dissenting justices wrote."Worse, the Court grants such extraordinary relief solely to allow the State to execute Pike before litigation over her conviction has properly run its course in the lower courts."Mental health considerationsThe case has sparked debate over capital punishment for young criminals.Pike was 18 when she and her boyfriend beat and killed Colleen Slemmer, 19, at a job training camp for young people.The killing gained national attention after Slemmer's body was found with a pentagram, often seen as a satanic symbol, carved in her chest.Pike's lawyers argued she should be granted clemency due to her young age and mental health issues at the time of the killing."She was 18 when she committed her crime, and she was deeply mentally ill," they wrote in a clemency petition to Tennessee Governor Bill Lee, who said he would not intervene.The US Supreme Court had rejected an application for a stay of execution on Tuesday, which argued that Pike's history as a victim of sexual assault, post-traumatic stress disorder and a blood condition meant a lethal injection would cause "needless suffering."Independent UN rights experts urged the US government and Tennessee authorities to "immediately halt" the execution and commute her death sentence."Pike's execution would mark the culmination of a trajectory of severe physical and psychological suffering marked by childhood abuse and nearly three decades of solitary confinement on death row," they said.In the United States, only 18 women have been executed since 1976, according to the Death Penalty Information Centre.The state of Tennessee will halt an execution planned for later this year after the failed attempt to end Pike's life, Governor Bill Lee said."The remaining scheduled execution will not be carried out this year," Lee was quoted as saying in a statement carried by the Tennessean and NewsNation, adding he was calling for a "comprehensive, third-party review" of the botched execution.

Photograph: Matthew Holst/Getty Images for MoveOn US healthcare Analysis Some conservative states aren’t using Medicaid hardship exemption – for political reasons Tobi Thomas Health and inequalities correspondent States like Missouri and Iowa are choosing to not take up exemption designed to help low-income people keep coverage during hardship Sun 18 Oct 2026 08.00 EDT Share Some conservative states that have rejected hardship exemptions for the new Medicaid requirements may be choosing not to due to political reasons, experts say. New federal work requirements for Medicaid, slated to come into effect on 1 January, mean that adults enrolled through the Affordable Care Act (ACA) Medicaid expansion will have to work, attend school, volunteer, or take part in another qualifying activity at least 80 hours a month to maintain their coverage. The bill also includes federal exemptions designed to help low-income people keep their Medicaid coverage when they are hospitalized, have to travel for medical care, or if they live in areas affected by disasters or high unemployment. Most recently, New York City has adopted the high-unemployment exemption for the Bronx, where about 200,000 residents would otherwise have been subject to the new requirements. However, some states like Missouri and Iowa are choosing not to take up this exemption for its residents, per new research by the healthcare policy nonprofit KFF, despite having counties that would qualify for this exemption. The Guardian has contacted both the Missouri and Iowa state departments for comment. Experts have noted to the Guardian why this could be the case – including states not wanting the extra administrative burden and varying political factors. Jennifer Tolbert, deputy director of KFF’s Program on Medicaid and the Uninsured, pointed to ideological opposition. “If [state officials] are advocates of work requirements, they may feel like these work requirements should apply to everyone evenly and whether someone lives in a county with high unemployment or not really shouldn’t be a factor,” Tolbert said. “It could also be an administrative burden, too, if the state were to adopt this hardship exception they have to submit the data on an ongoing basis to CMS and then they have to make sure their system, their eligibility system is able to blanket exempt or exclude people from these work requirements based on where they live and they’re living in a particular county. So that could be a factor as well.” Sarah H Gordon, associate professor at the Boston University School of Public Health, also pointed to politics coming into play behind these states’ decisions. “States that are not taking up the hardship exemption tend to be more politically conservative states that typically align with the idea that health insurance should be tied to employment or other community engagement activities,” Gordon said. “Medicaid is a federal program and there is a lot of variation between states.” She added: “Not taking up that exemption is partly political. We have states that are taking up work requirements early, states that are taking less time to make sure they understand the new requirements. This is just a patchwork of implementation where some states are going above and beyond to try and minimize coverage losses and other states really aren’t and way more people will lose coverage.” Joel Ferber, director of advocacy at Legal Services of Eastern Missouri, said that it was “disappointing” that the state was not currently planing to take up these exemptions that could potentially benefit its residents. “They say that they are not because they don’t want to create additional bureaucratic burdens of its participants, but this doesn’t make sense. “If you polled Medicaid participants and said to them, would you rather lose your healthcare or fill out a hardship form, 100% of them would likely choose to fill out the form. So it just doesn’t make sense,” he continued. Most notably, the introduction of these new requirements will result in millions of Americans losing their healthcare coverage. A clear example of this policy in action is in Arkansas, which introduced Medicaid work requirements in 2018. By the end of that year, more than 18,000 people had lost coverage, yet researchers found no significant increase in employment. Jacob Wallace, associate professor at the Yale School of Public Health and an expert on Medicaid, called the new work requirements “very concerning”. “Historically, they don’t encourage people to work, but they do seem to generate administrative burdens and paperwork that leads to people dropping off the program,” Wallace said. “There’s a very broad concern about the loss of coverage that is likely to happen, and hopefully states are trying to mitigate those losses as best as they can.” He added: “And the more hoops we ask people to jump through to exempt themselves or qualify themselves for work requirements, the more people we lose just because we don’t have the right address, or phone number. We send the paperwork but it’s confusing and we don’t provide enough support for people to do the paperwork.” Explore more on these topics US healthcare Iowa Missouri analysis Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed US news US politics Midterms 2026 World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine US immigration Soccer Business Environment Tech Science Newsletters The Filter Wellness

https://www.euronews.com/2026/10/27/unac.text: Jordan said on Tuesday that airstrikes on Syria had killed around 20 Islamic State militants as it acknowledged that there had also been a number of civilian casualties.The Jordanian armed forces launched a wave of strikes against southern Syria on Monday evening, targeting what it said were "hideouts of terrorist organisations.""RJAF fighter jets destroyed a number of terrorist locations, killing and wounding several terrorists and destroying their equipment," the military said in a statement, adding that the operation had been carried out "in retaliation" for a recent attack on a Greek Orthodox church in Karak that reportedly killed nine people.Government spokesperson Mohammad Al-Momani said the operation had resulted in the deaths of more than 20 IS operatives as well as the destruction of a "major" weapons depot. He said the strikes had been conducted following intelligence on "imminent terrorist threats."Al-Momani added that Jordan had "avoided" civilian sites and that it regretted "unintended casualties" as he stressed that the country had "deep respect" for the Syrian state and people.Syria's foreign ministry has condemned the strikes, calling them an "unacceptable violation and breach of Syrian airspace without any prior coordination."Syria's civil defence agency put the death toll at seven people.In the Daraa Governorate, an airstrike killed five people from the same family - three children, a woman and a man - the agency said in a post on social media.An 80-year-old was also killed in strikes on Daraa while a 60-year-old was killed in the Suwayda Governorate, it said."We were asleep when the missile hit us. My mother, my older brother and his three children -- two boys and a girl -- were killed," said Nassouh al-Salim in the village of Al-Taf in the Daraa region, per the AFP news agency.
